You answer a question about machines at work (law, guidance, manufacturers' manuals, company and plant
documents) using ONLY the numbered passages given. Each passage is headed by its document, its place and its rank.

Rules:
- Use only the passages. Do not use anything you know from elsewhere.
- Answer only if a passage states the answer for the exact subject asked about (the same device, the same article
  and paragraph, the same kind of verification, the same deadline). A passage about a neighbouring subject does not
  answer the question: then the kind is "unknown" and the value is null. A question about something that happened
  (the date of the last check, whether something is overdue today) is "unknown" unless a passage records that event.
- A passage marked "corrected by the corrigendum" already shows the corrected wording: reason with it. The old
  wording, given in the mark, is no longer valid.
- If the question asks about a day, compare that day with every date in the passages, one by one. A repeal or an
  application "from" a date takes effect on that date, not earlier: an act repealed from a date is still fully in
  force on every earlier day; a rule applying from a date does not yet bind on earlier days.
- When passages of different rank disagree, the higher rank wins: law, then guidance, then manufacturer's manual,
  then company procedure, then plant record. Between two Italian texts, a legislative decree (D.Lgs.) wins over a
  ministerial decree (DM). Say which one wins.
- A row of a table belongs to the thing named in that same row. Read the row of the item asked about, not a
  neighbouring row. When the question itself states a condition ("if it were in regular use", "built in 2017"),
  reason with that condition.
- The kind follows the question: "from which date / by which date / when (a day)" is "date"; "how often / for how
  long / within what time" is "duration"; "can / may / is / does / must" is "boolean"; "which / what (several
  things)" is "set"; who, why, under which condition is "text" (one short sentence naming every element asked for).
- Point at the evidence: for every passage you rely on, copy word for word the sentence, or the table row, that
  states what you use. Copy exactly, without changing a character; do not join text from two places.
- Return JSON only, with the reasoning first:
  {"reasoning": "what the passages say and how it leads to the answer, in a few short sentences",
   "kind": "set|date|duration|boolean|text|unknown",
   "value": <list of short strings for set | "YYYY-MM-DD" for date | ISO 8601 duration like "P10Y", "P6M", "P45D", "PT1H" | true/false | a short text | null>,
   "text": "one or two sentences for a person, naming the document and the article, section or page",
   "evidence": [{"passage": <number>, "quote": "<copied exactly from that passage>"}]}

Assembly and Mounting Dimensionin The magnitude of the loads depends on robot model, program and multiple other factors. g the Stand Dimensioning of the stand shall account for the loads that the robot arm generates during normal uninterrupted operation and during category 0, 1 and 2 stopping motion. During stopping motion, the joints are allowed to exceed the maximum nominal operating torque. The load during stopping motion is independent of the stop category type. The values stated in the following tables are maximum nominal loads in worst-case movements multiplied with a safety factor of 2.5. The actual loads will not exceed these values. Robot Model Mz [Nm] Fz[N] Mxy[Nm] Fxy [N] UR5e 450 1090 750 910 Maximum joint torques during category 0, 1 and 2 stops. Robot Model Mz [Nm] Fz[N] Mxy[Nm] Fxy [N] UR5e 380 950 630 750 Maximum joint torques during normal operation. Copyright © 2009–2025 by Universal Robots A/S. All rights reserved. The normal operating loads can generally be reduced by lowering the acceleration limits of the joints. Actual operating loads are dependent on the application and robot program. You can use URSim to evaluate the expected loads in your specific application. Safety You can incorporate added safety margins, factoring in the following design considerations: margin s • Static stiffness: A stand that is not sufficiently stiff will deflect during robot motion, resulting in the robot arm not hitting the intended waypoint or path. Lack of static stiffness can also result in a poor freedrive teaching experience or protective stops. • Dynamic stiffness: If the frequency of the stand matches the movement frequency of the robot arm, the entire system can resonate, creating the impression that the robot arm is vibrating. Lack of dynamic stiffness can also result in protective stops. The stand should have a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz. • Fatigue: The stand shall be dimensioned to match the expected operating lifetime and load cycles of the complete system. WARNING • Potential for tip-over Hazards. • The robot arm's operational loads can cause movable platforms, such as tables or mobile robots, to tip over, resulting in possible accidents. • Prioritize safety by implementing adequate measures to prevent the tipping of movable platforms at all times. CAUTION • If the robot is mounted on an external axis, the accelerations of this axis must not be too high. You can let the robot software compensate for the acceleration of external axes by using script command: set_base_acceleration() • High accelerations can cause the robot to make safety stops. If this condition is ignored, the load nut may break through as wear progresses. In this case, the downstream safety nut takes over the load completely and the vehicle can be lowered, but it cannot be raised again from the home position. The following dimensions must be observed: Upper edge of threaded pin (A) is flush with upper edge of New condition support plate (B). Threaded pin protrudes ≥ 3 mm above support plate.
